Spanish numbers, by the value they name.cinco: Its cousin 'cinco de Mayo' marks a Mexican victory at Puebla in 1862, and the word comes from Latin 'quinque', root of 'quintet'.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.doce: From Latin 'duodecim'. Spanish has unique words up to quince (15), then switches to 'dieci-' compounds like dieciséis.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.quince: A girl's quinceañera at 15 is a major coming-of-age celebration across Latin America, with a formal dress, a dance and a big party.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.veinte: From Latin 'viginti'. Numbers 21 to 29 fuse into one word, like veintiuno, whereas higher tens stay as separate words.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.treinta: From Latin 'triginta'. Past 30, Spanish splits numbers into three words, as in treinta y uno, unlike the fused 21 to 29.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.cincuenta: Built on cinco plus the -enta ending Spanish uses for 30 through 90, so once you know cinco the pattern is easy to spot.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.setenta: Siete shrinks to set- here, just as nueve shrinks to nov- in noventa, so these two tens don't match their unit words exactly.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.noventa: From Latin 'nonaginta'. Ninety is the last of the -enta tens before Spanish jumps to the round number cien.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.cien: Cien becomes ciento when more follows, as in ciento uno. The same Latin root gave English 'century' and 'percent'.
Spanish numbers, by the value they name.mil: Spanish needs no 'one' in front: 1,000 is simply mil. It comes from Latin 'mille', which also gave English 'mile' and 'millennium'.

Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Penitential Act: Congregation admits sin: 'I confess to almighty God' (the Confiteor) or the Kyrie 'Lord, have mercy' follows the greeting.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Gloria: This ancient hymn begins with the angels' words to the shepherds in Luke, and is omitted during Advent and Lent.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.First Reading: Usually from the Old Testament, though in the Easter season it comes from the Acts of the Apostles.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Gospel: The congregation stands, and many trace small crosses on forehead, lips and heart.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Homily: A short sermon explaining the readings, given by the priest or deacon, and it is expected on Sundays.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Creed: This is the Nicene Creed, whose text was drafted at councils in Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Eucharistic Prayer: The heart of the Mass, when bread and wine are consecrated, including words from the Last Supper.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Lord's Prayer: In the Mass, the people add 'For the kingdom, the power and the glory' after the priest's extra prayer.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Sign of Peace: Worshippers exchange a handshake or greeting, echoing the early Christian kiss of peace.
Parts of the Catholic Mass, in order.Dismissal: The word 'Mass' is thought to derive from the Latin 'Ite, missa est', the words of the dismissal.

How long until it breaks down?.Paper towel: Mostly cellulose, it breaks down quickly because microbes eat it, as long as it is not coated or plastic-laminated.
How long until it breaks down?.Apple core: Fruit scraps vanish quickly because microbes and insects feast on the sugars, unlike the plastic wrappers around them.
How long until it breaks down?.Wool sock: Wool is a protein, keratin, just like hair, so in soil it feeds fungi and bacteria and even releases nitrogen.
How long until it breaks down?.Plastic bag: Thin bags may break into microplastics instead of truly vanishing, and these estimates vary widely.
How long until it breaks down?.Nylon fabric: The first fully synthetic fibre, introduced by DuPont in the 1930s, it sheds microfibres when washed.
How long until it breaks down?.Tin can: The can was patented in 1810, decades before the can opener, so early soldiers opened them with bayonets.
How long until it breaks down?.Aluminum can: Recycling one saves about 95 percent of the energy needed to make a new one.
How long until it breaks down?.Plastic bottle: PET bottles can be recycled into fleece clothing, though few are.
How long until it breaks down?.Fishing line: Monofilament line is a major ocean hazard, entangling turtles, seabirds and marine mammals.
How long until it breaks down?.Glass bottle: Glass is made of silica sand and can be recycled endlessly without losing quality.

Cricket greats, by Test debut.Don Bradman: Don Bradman's Test average of 99.94 is the best in history, and in his final innings he needed just four runs to get 100 and was out for a duck.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Garfield Sobers: Garry Sobers hit six sixes in one over in first-class cricket in 1968, and he was an outstanding all-rounder.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Sunil Gavaskar: Sunil Gavaskar was the first batsman to score 10,000 Test runs, and he often faced the fearsome West Indian pace attack without a helmet.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Viv Richards: Viv Richards was the swaggering West Indian batsman who famously never wore a helmet, and he captained a team that went unbeaten for years.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Ian Botham: Ian Botham's Ashes heroics in 1981 made it Botham's Ashes, and he combined fiery batting with swing bowling.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Sachin Tendulkar: Sachin Tendulkar debuted at 16 and went on to score 100 international centuries, and fans called him the Little Master.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Brian Lara: Brian Lara holds the highest individual Test score of 400 not out and the highest first-class score of 501, both set in 1994 and 2004.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Shane Warne: Shane Warne's first ball in Ashes cricket, to Mike Gatting, is called the Ball of the Century, as it spun hugely.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Ricky Ponting: Ricky Ponting captained Australia to two World Cups and was known for his aggressive style, especially the pull shot.
Cricket greats, by Test debut.Virat Kohli: Virat Kohli debuted in 2011 and became one of the greatest batsmen of the modern era, famous for chasing down totals.

Milestones in wireless communication.Marconi's transatlantic signal: Marconi's transatlantic signal was the letter S in Morse code, sent from Cornwall to Newfoundland, and it proved radio could cross oceans.
Milestones in wireless communication.First radio broadcast: Reginald Fessenden made the first radio broadcast of voice and music, and it was heard by ships' operators on Christmas Eve.
Milestones in wireless communication.First handheld cellphone call: Martin Cooper made the first handheld cell call in 1973, and he phoned a rival at Bell Labs, and the phone weighed over a kilogram.
Milestones in wireless communication.First 1G network: The first 1G network, launched in Japan, used analog signals, and it supported only voice.
Milestones in wireless communication.First GSM call: The first GSM call was made in Finland, and GSM became the global standard for second-generation mobile phones.
Milestones in wireless communication.Wi-Fi standard (802.11): The 802.11 standard laid the foundation for Wi-Fi, and the name Wi-Fi was invented by a branding agency.
Milestones in wireless communication.First 3G network: The first commercial 3G network launched in Japan, and it brought video calls and mobile web.
Milestones in wireless communication.First 4G LTE network: The first 4G LTE networks launched in Stockholm and Oslo, and they enabled fast mobile streaming.
Milestones in wireless communication.First 5G networks: The first 5G networks began in 2019, and they promise ultra-fast speeds and lower latency.
Milestones in wireless communication.Starlink public beta: Starlink's public beta began in late 2020, and its satellites are visible as a string of lights in the night sky.

Great chemists, by birth year.Robert Boyle: Robert Boyle formulated Boyle's law relating gas pressure and volume, and he's often called the father of modern chemistry.
Great chemists, by birth year.Henry Cavendish: Henry Cavendish discovered hydrogen, and he was so shy that he communicated with his servants by notes.
Great chemists, by birth year.Antoine Lavoisier: Antoine Lavoisier named oxygen and helped establish the law of conservation of mass, and he was guillotined in the French Revolution.
Great chemists, by birth year.John Dalton: John Dalton proposed modern atomic theory, and he was color-blind, and he first described the condition.
Great chemists, by birth year.Humphry Davy: Humphry Davy discovered several elements through electrolysis, and he also invented a miner's safety lamp.
Great chemists, by birth year.August Kekulé: August Kekule claimed that he discovered benzene's ring structure after dreaming of a snake biting its tail.
Great chemists, by birth year.Dmitri Mendeleev: Dmitri Mendeleev built the periodic table and left gaps for elements not yet discovered, and later ones fit his predictions.
Great chemists, by birth year.Fritz Haber: Fritz Haber invented a way to make ammonia from air, which feeds billions, and also pioneered chemical weapons in World War I.
Great chemists, by birth year.Linus Pauling: Linus Pauling won two unshared Nobel Prizes, in Chemistry and Peace, and he championed vitamin C.
Great chemists, by birth year.Glenn Seaborg: Glenn Seaborg helped discover ten elements, and element 106 was named seaborgium while he was alive.

James Bond's cars, by film year.Aston Martin DB5: Aston Martin DB5 in Goldfinger, with its ejector seat and revolving plates, became so iconic that a toy version sold in huge numbers.
James Bond's cars, by film year.Toyota 2000GT: Only two open-top versions were built for You Only Live Twice, reportedly because Sean Connery was too tall for the coupe.
James Bond's cars, by film year.Ford Mustang Mach 1: The film's Las Vegas chase features a famous tilted drive on two wheels, entering one side of an alley and exiting on the other.
James Bond's cars, by film year.Lotus Esprit submarine car: In The Spy Who Loved Me, Bond drives off a pier and the car turns into a submarine, with fins and a periscope.
James Bond's cars, by film year.Aston Martin V8 Vantage: In The Living Daylights it gets skis, outriggers and a rocket booster, perfect for escaping across a frozen lake.
James Bond's cars, by film year.BMW Z3: The roadster appeared in only a few scenes of GoldenEye, but the placement was a coup for BMW.
James Bond's cars, by film year.BMW Z8: In The World Is Not Enough, a helicopter with a dangling saw slices it clean in half.
James Bond's cars, by film year.Aston Martin Vanquish: Die Another Day gave it an invisibility cloak, but the 'Vanish' gadget was not enough to keep it out of an ice duel.
James Bond's cars, by film year.Aston Martin DBS: Bond wins it in a card game in Casino Royale, and its stunt car set a world record with seven barrel rolls.
James Bond's cars, by film year.Aston Martin DB10: Only ten were built, solely for the film Spectre, and none were sold to the public.

Paper sizes, by area.B8: The ISO B series sits between A sizes, since each B is the geometric mean of the neighboring A sizes, and B8 is about the size of a small playing card.
Paper sizes, by area.A7: A7 is roughly the size of a playing card, and, like all A sizes, it has sides in the ratio of the square root of 2.
Paper sizes, by area.B7: B7 is used for things like passports, and the B series is mostly used for posters, books, and envelopes.
Paper sizes, by area.A6: A6 is about the size of a postcard, and it is one quarter of an A4 sheet, so four A6 fit exactly on A4.
Paper sizes, by area.B6: B6 is a common size for paperback books and notebooks, especially in Japan.
Paper sizes, by area.A5: A5 is half of A4, and it is a favorite size for notebooks and planners.
Paper sizes, by area.B5: B5 is widely used for notebooks in Japan, and it falls between A5 and A4 in size.
Paper sizes, by area.A4: A4 is the world's most-used paper size outside North America, and it is based on a one-square-meter sheet, A0, folded in half over and over.
Paper sizes, by area.B4: B4 is a bit bigger than A4, and Japan's JIS version of it is slightly different from the ISO one.
Paper sizes, by area.A3: A3 is exactly two A4 sheets and is the biggest size the normal office printer can use, often used for posters and drawings.

Turning points in Japanese history.Battle of Sekigahara: At Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated rival warlords, and three years later he became shogun, founding a regime that lasted over 250 years.
Turning points in Japanese history.Perry's Black Ships arrive: Commodore Perry's steamships forced Japan to open to trade after more than two centuries of isolation, and the black color was thought an omen.
Turning points in Japanese history.Meiji Restoration: The Meiji Restoration returned the emperor to power and set off rapid industrialization, ending the samurai class.
Turning points in Japanese history.First Sino-Japanese War: Japan's win in the First Sino-Japanese War made it the dominant power in East Asia, and it gained Taiwan.
Turning points in Japanese history.Russo-Japanese War: Japan's surprise victory over Russia was the first time in modern history that an Asian power defeated a European one.
Turning points in Japanese history.Great Kanto earthquake: The Great Kanto earthquake struck Tokyo and Yokohama and killed over 100,000 people, and caused fires that burned for days.
Turning points in Japanese history.Attack on Pearl Harbor: The attack on Pearl Harbor drew the United States into the Second World War, and Japan had been planning it for months.
Turning points in Japanese history.Hiroshima bombing: The atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima killed tens of thousands instantly, and the city was later rebuilt as a 'peace city'.
Turning points in Japanese history.Tokyo hosts the Olympics: The Tokyo Olympics came less than 20 years after the war, and the Shinkansen bullet train began running in time for them.
Turning points in Japanese history.Kobe earthquake: The Kobe earthquake killed over 6,000 people, and it led Japan to rethink its building codes and disaster response.

Shopping innovations, by debut year.Montgomery Ward mail catalog: Aaron Montgomery Ward's 1872 one-page price sheet launched mail order, with the promise 'satisfaction guaranteed or your money back'.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.Cash register: Saloon owner James Ritty invented it in Dayton, Ohio, to stop his staff stealing, and early models rang a bell on each sale.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.Self-service grocery store: Piggly Wiggly in Memphis let customers pick goods off shelves themselves instead of asking a clerk.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.Parking meter: Carl Magee invented them to stop all-day parking in Oklahoma City, and the first were installed there in 1935.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.Shopping cart: Sylvan Goldman of Oklahoma City invented it, and shoppers were at first so shy of them that he hired people to push them around.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.QVC shopping channel: Its name stands for Quality, Value, Convenience, and it sold its goods around the clock on live TV.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.Mall of America: Based in Minnesota, it holds a full indoor theme park, and was among the largest malls in America.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.Tesco Clubcard: It was among Britain's first major loyalty cards, and the shopper data it generated helped Tesco overtake its rivals.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.Amazon Prime: It launched with free two-day shipping for a fee of 79 dollars a year, a deal that was widely doubted at the time.
Shopping innovations, by debut year.Amazon Go store: The cashier-free store in Seattle used cameras and sensors, with its 'Just Walk Out' technology, to charge shoppers as they left.

Milestones in chemistry.Boyle's The Sceptical Chymist: Robert Boyle challenged the old four-element idea and argued elements should be defined by experiment, helping chemistry break away from alchemy.
Milestones in chemistry.Lavoisier names oxygen: Lavoisier showed oxygen is what burns in air and named it from Greek for acid-former, mistakenly believing it was in every acid.
Milestones in chemistry.Dalton's atomic theory: John Dalton proposed that each element is made of identical atoms with a characteristic weight, giving chemistry its first quantitative atomic model.
Milestones in chemistry.Wöhler synthesizes urea: Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a compound of living things, from inorganic ingredients, undermining the belief that organic matter needed a mysterious vital force.
Milestones in chemistry.Kekulé's benzene ring: Kekulé said he pictured benzene's ring after daydreaming of a snake biting its own tail, though historians debate how true the story is.
Milestones in chemistry.Mendeleev's periodic table: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties; gallium, scandium and germanium later matched his forecasts.
Milestones in chemistry.Haber process: Fritz Haber's way of turning nitrogen from air into ammonia makes fertilizer that helps feed roughly half of humanity; it also made explosives cheaper.
Milestones in chemistry.Pauling's chemical bond: Linus Pauling's book on the chemical bond applied quantum mechanics to molecules and helped win him the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Milestones in chemistry.Buckyball discovered: C60 is a soccer-ball-shaped molecule of 60 carbon atoms, named for Buckminster Fuller's domes; its discoverers won the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Milestones in chemistry.Element 118 named: Oganesson was named for Yuri Oganessian, only the second element named for a living person, and it is the heaviest element known.

Units of energy.Joule: Named for brewer-turned-physicist James Prescott Joule; one joule is about the energy to lift a small apple one meter.
Units of energy.Foot-pound: It is the energy needed to lift one pound by one foot, and it shares units with torque despite being unrelated.
Units of energy.Calorie (small): The small calorie warms a gram of water by one degree Celsius; the Calorie on food labels is a thousand of these.
Units of energy.BTU: A British thermal unit heats a pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit, and is still used for air conditioners and furnaces.
Units of energy.Watt-hour: One watt for an hour; a typical phone battery holds around 10 to 15 of them.
Units of energy.Kilocalorie (food): The Calorie on food labels is really this, and one is about 4.2 kilojoules.
Units of energy.Kilowatt-hour: This is what your electricity bill charges for, and a typical US home uses around 10,000 a year.
Units of energy.Therm: Equal to 100,000 BTU, this unit is used to bill natural gas in the US and UK.
Units of energy.Ton of TNT: Defined as exactly 4.184 gigajoules, whatever a real ton of TNT would yield, it is the standard comparison for explosions.
Units of energy.Barrel of oil equivalent: A 42-gallon barrel of crude holds this energy; the barrel size dates from the Pennsylvania oil boom.

How long they held the top job.Liz Truss (UK PM): Her 2022 mini-budget rattled markets and the pound, and she resigned after 49 days; a tabloid's lettuce livestream famously outlasted her.
How long they held the top job.Edward VIII (king): He abdicated in December 1936 to marry twice-divorced American Wallis Simpson, becoming Duke of Windsor and handing the crown to his brother George VI.
How long they held the top job.John F. Kennedy (president): At 43 he was the youngest person elected US president and the first Catholic one; he was assassinated in Dallas in November 1963.
How long they held the top job.Barack Obama (president): He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2009, early in his first term, and was the first Black president of the United States.
How long they held the top job.Margaret Thatcher (UK PM): Britain's first female prime minister won three straight elections, and her unbroken run in office was the longest of the 20th century.
How long they held the top job.Angela Merkel (chancellor): A physicist with a doctorate who grew up in East Germany, she led Germany from 2005 and stepped down voluntarily in 2021.
How long they held the top job.John Paul II (pope): Born Karol Wojtyła in Poland, he was the first non-Italian pope in over 450 years and traveled to well over 100 countries.
How long they held the top job.Queen Victoria: Her reign gave a whole era its name, and she also held the title Empress of India; she took the throne at 18 in 1837.
How long they held the top job.Queen Elizabeth II: She became queen at 25 in 1952 and in 2015 passed Victoria's record to become Britain's longest-reigning monarch.
How long they held the top job.Louis XIV of France: The Sun King took the throne at four, built the palace of Versailles, and reigned longer than any other known European monarch.

Frequencies in everyday life.UK mains electricity: The grid is kept near 50 Hz, and it dips slightly when demand surges, such as when millions put kettles on after a big TV show.
Frequencies in everyday life.Middle C on a piano: It's called 'middle' because it sits near the middle of the keyboard, and on a ledger line between the two staves of piano music.
Frequencies in everyday life.Concert A tuning note: The dial tone on North American phones is a mix of two pitches, 350 Hz and 440 Hz.
Frequencies in everyday life.Top of human hearing: Children can hear it, but hearing gradually fades from the top down as we age, a process called presbycusis.
Frequencies in everyday life.AM radio station: At night AM waves bounce off the upper atmosphere, so you can pick up stations from hundreds of kilometres away.
Frequencies in everyday life.FM radio station: FM resists static better than AM and has the bandwidth for stereo, so music stations gravitated to it.
Frequencies in everyday life.GPS signal: Satellite clocks run slightly fast compared with the ground, and without relativity corrections GPS would drift by about ten kilometres a day.
Frequencies in everyday life.Microwave oven: The mesh in the door has holes smaller than the 12 cm wavelength, so waves stay in but light lets you watch.
Frequencies in everyday life.Wi-Fi, faster band: The 5 GHz band carries more data but is absorbed more by walls, so its range is shorter than the 2.4 GHz band.
Frequencies in everyday life.Green light: Visible light runs from roughly 430 THz for red up to 750 THz for violet, and green sits near the middle.

Age at time of spaceflight.Gherman Titov: His flight of over a day made him the first to sleep in space and the first to suffer space sickness.
Age at time of spaceflight.Valentina Tereshkova: She was the first woman in space, in 1963, and remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.
Age at time of spaceflight.Yuri Gagarin: His 108-minute orbit in 1961 made him the first human in space, and he ejected and parachuted down separately from his capsule.
Age at time of spaceflight.Sally Ride (first flight): In 1983 she became the first American woman in space. She later also served on the board investigating the Challenger accident.
Age at time of spaceflight.Neil Armstrong (Apollo 11): He took manual control to avoid a boulder field on the Moon, with only around 25 seconds of fuel left.
Age at time of spaceflight.John Glenn (1962): He was the first American to orbit Earth, completing three orbits in Friendship 7.
Age at time of spaceflight.Dennis Tito: The first paying space tourist reportedly paid about 20 million dollars to visit the International Space Station in 2001.
Age at time of spaceflight.John Glenn (1998): At 77 he became the oldest astronaut, and flew a Shuttle mission partly to study how ageing and spaceflight compare.
Age at time of spaceflight.Wally Funk: She trained for spaceflight in the early 1960s, but was never selected, and finally flew on Blue Origin in 2021.
Age at time of spaceflight.William Shatner: The actor who played Captain Kirk flew on a roughly 10-minute Blue Origin hop in 2021, becoming the oldest person to reach space.

Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᚠ Fehu: It means cattle or wealth. The runic alphabet is called futhark after its first six letters, F U Th A R K.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᚦ Thurisaz: It means giant, and it inspired the Old English letter thorn.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᚱ Raidho: It means ride or journey, and it is the ancestor of the letter R.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᚷ Gebo: It means gift, and its X shape is among the simplest runes, two crossing strokes.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᚺ Hagalaz: It means hail, the weather that could wreck a harvest, and it is the ancestor of H.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᛁ Isa: It means ice, and is just a single vertical stroke.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᛃ Jera: It means year or harvest, and is related to English year and German Jahr.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᛊ Sowilo: It means sun, and its zigzag shape stands for the s sound.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᛒ Berkano: It means birch, and its two bumps are the ancestor of the letter B.
Elder Futhark runes, in rune-row order.ᛚ Laguz: It means water or lake, the ancestor of L, and the Elder Futhark was used in Germanic lands for centuries.

One classic album for each year of the 1.Bridge Over Troubled Water: It was the last album by Simon and Garfunkel, and its title song won them big at the Grammys.
One classic album for each year of the 1.Led Zeppelin IV: The band left the album untitled, using four symbols, and Stairway to Heaven was never released as a single.
One classic album for each year of the 1.Ziggy Stardust: Bowie's alien rock star persona Ziggy lasted just about a year before he retired the character on stage.
One classic album for each year of the 1.Goodbye Yellow Brick Road: The double album includes Candle in the Wind, written about Marilyn Monroe and later reworked for Princess Diana.
One classic album for each year of the 1.Diamond Dogs: Bowie planned a musical of Orwell's 1984, but when the rights were refused, the songs turned into this album.
One classic album for each year of the 1.Born to Run: Springsteen took about six months to record the title track, and he made the covers of Time and Newsweek in one week.
One classic album for each year of the 1.Hotel California: The cover shows the Beverly Hills Hotel, and the song is often read as a parable about excess in 1970s California.
One classic album for each year of the 1.Bat Out of Hell: Jim Steinman's operatic rock was turned down by many labels, but it went on to sell over 40 million copies.
One classic album for each year of the 1.Parallel Lines (Blondie): Heart of Glass blended punk with disco and carried the band into the mainstream.
One classic album for each year of the 1.London Calling: The cover shows Paul Simonon smashing his bass, which echoed Elvis Presley's first album cover.

Famous inventors, by birth year.Johannes Gutenberg: The German goldsmith's movable type printing press around 1450 made books affordable, and his Bible is among the most valuable books.
Famous inventors, by birth year.Leonardo da Vinci: Born in the village of Vinci, he sketched flying machines and tanks, and wrote his notes in mirror writing.
Famous inventors, by birth year.Benjamin Franklin: He invented the lightning rod and bifocals, and he proposed that lightning is electricity.
Famous inventors, by birth year.James Watt: He improved the steam engine and coined horsepower, and the watt is named after him.
Famous inventors, by birth year.Alfred Nobel: A premature newspaper obituary, which mistook his death for his brother's, is said to have inspired his prizes.
Famous inventors, by birth year.Alexander Graham Bell: He taught deaf students, his wife Mabel was deaf, and he won the first US telephone patent in 1876.
Famous inventors, by birth year.George Eastman (Kodak): His company's slogan was You press the button, we do the rest, and his Kodak made photography available to everyone.
Famous inventors, by birth year.Henry Ford: His moving assembly line in 1913 cut the time to build a Model T from many hours to about an hour and a half.
Famous inventors, by birth year.Orville Wright: He piloted the first powered flight in 1903, while his older brother Wilbur was the elder of the two.
Famous inventors, by birth year.Guglielmo Marconi: His wireless sets helped save survivors of the Titanic, as operators on the Carpathia heard the distress call.

Calories: from nothing to a feast.Glass of water: Water has no calories, but your own body is roughly 60 percent water.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.A Tic Tac: Tic Tac labels may say zero calories because one mint weighs about half a gram, small enough for rounding rules.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.Hard-boiled egg: Roughly 6 grams of protein sit in one egg, and the yolk holds most of its vitamins and minerals.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.Glass of orange juice: A glass has the sugar of several oranges with almost none of the fibre, which is why dietitians suggest eating the fruit.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.Pint of lager: Alcohol contains about 7 calories per gram, nearly as much as fat's 9, so beer's energy comes largely from the alcohol.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.Slice of cheese pizza: Neapolitan pizza-making was added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2017.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.Big Mac: Since 1986, The Economist has used its price in different countries as a light-hearted gauge of whether currencies are valued fairly.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.Typical daily intake guide: The 2,000-calorie figure is a rounded reference used on US food labels; real needs vary with age, size and activity.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.Whole large pizza: A large pizza eaten whole can top an entire day's recommended intake, which is why people split it.
Calories: from nothing to a feast.Michael Phelps' legendary diet: Phelps later played down the famous number as exaggerated, though elite training did demand several times a normal intake.

When these algorithms were devised.Euclid's GCD algorithm: It appears in Euclid's Elements, and is often called the oldest algorithm still in common use.
When these algorithms were devised.Sieve of Eratosthenes: Eratosthenes, who also measured Earth's circumference, listed primes by crossing out multiples.
When these algorithms were devised.Al-Khwarizmi's algebra: The word 'algorithm' derives from his name, and 'algebra' from al-jabr in his book.
When these algorithms were devised.Merge sort: John von Neumann devised it in 1945, splitting lists in half and merging them back in order.
When these algorithms were devised.Quicksort: Tony Hoare devised it in 1959 as a student in Moscow, sorting words for machine translation.
When these algorithms were devised.Fast Fourier transform: Cooley and Tukey published it in 1965, though Gauss had a similar idea in 1805; it underlies audio compression.
When these algorithms were devised.Diffie-Hellman key exchange: It let two strangers agree on a secret key over a public channel, a first step to public-key cryptography.
When these algorithms were devised.RSA: Its security rests on the difficulty of factoring large numbers; Britain's GCHQ had discovered it in secret earlier.
When these algorithms were devised.Backpropagation (popularized): Popularized by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, it trains neural networks, the foundation of modern AI.
When these algorithms were devised.PageRank: Larry Page and Sergey Brin ranked pages by incoming links, and the name is partly a pun on Page's surname.

When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Wilhelm Röntgen: Won the very first Physics Nobel for discovering X-rays, and refused to patent them.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Ivan Pavlov: Won the Physiology or Medicine prize for digestion research, not for his famous dogs and bells.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Ernest Rutherford: He won the Chemistry prize, not Physics, for work on radioactivity.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Max Planck: Won for founding quantum theory, which he reluctantly introduced to solve a problem about hot objects.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Albert Einstein: His Nobel was for the photoelectric effect, not relativity.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Niels Bohr: Won for his model of the atom. Element 107, bohrium, is named after him.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Paul Dirac: Shared the prize with Schrodinger, and his equation predicted antimatter.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Enrico Fermi: Won for work on neutron-induced radioactivity, then used the Stockholm trip to leave fascist Italy.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Richard Feynman: Shared with Tomonaga and Schwinger for quantum electrodynamics.
When these scientists won their Nobel Pr.Peter Higgs: Shared the prize with Francois Englert for the Higgs boson, found at CERN in 2012.

How long can they hold their breath?.Human (untrained): Untrained people manage about a minute, but free divers who breathe pure oxygen first have held on for over 20 minutes.
How long can they hold their breath?.Sea otter: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal, with up to a million hairs per square inch, which traps air for warmth.
How long can they hold their breath?.Bottlenose dolphin: Dolphins slow their heart rate on dives and rely on oxygen stored in blood and muscle, rather than big lungs.
How long can they hold their breath?.Beaver: A beaver's ears and nostrils close underwater, and its transparent eyelids act like goggles while it swims.
How long can they hold their breath?.Manatee: Manatees are mostly resting underwater, surfacing every few minutes for air, and they're related to elephants.
How long can they hold their breath?.Emperor penguin: Emperor penguins dive for fish below 500 meters, deeper than any other bird, and can stay under for over 20 minutes.
How long can they hold their breath?.Sperm whale: Sperm whales dive for squid thousands of feet down, with muscles that store huge amounts of oxygen.
How long can they hold their breath?.Elephant seal: Elephant seals can stay underwater for hours while hunting, though most dives last under half an hour.
How long can they hold their breath?.Cuvier's beaked whale: This beaked whale holds the mammal record at 3 h 42 min, and also dives near 3 km deep, hunting squid in the dark.
How long can they hold their breath?.Green sea turtle (resting): Resting turtles drastically slow their heart and metabolism, which lets them stay under for hours between breaths.

When these music genres were born.Polka: The lively dance came from Bohemia, now Czechia, and spread across Europe and the Americas within decades.
When these music genres were born.Ragtime: Scott Joplin's 'Maple Leaf Rag' made it famous; its syncopated, 'ragged' rhythm set the stage for jazz.
When these music genres were born.Jazz: New Orleans is often credited as its birthplace, mixing blues, ragtime and brass bands with improvisation at its heart.
When these music genres were born.Swing: Big bands led by Benny Goodman and Duke Ellington made it the pop music of its day, and fueled the Lindy Hop craze.
When these music genres were born.Bebop: Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie played fast, complex improvisations that were music for listening rather than dancing.
When these music genres were born.Rock and roll: Elvis, Chuck Berry and Little Richard fused rhythm and blues with country, and DJ Alan Freed helped popularize the name.
When these music genres were born.Reggae: Born in Jamaica from ska and rocksteady, its offbeat guitar chop was carried worldwide by Bob Marley.
When these music genres were born.Hip hop: Said to have been born at a Bronx party where DJ Kool Herc extended the drum breaks; a 1973 block party is its traditional birthday.
When these music genres were born.Grunge: From Seattle, it blended punk and metal; Nirvana's Nevermind in 1991 pushed it into the mainstream.
When these music genres were born.Dubstep: Born in South London clubs, it is defined by heavy sub-bass and sparse drums, and went mainstream through Skrillex.

Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.deca-: Deca means 'ten' and is rarely used, though the decade and decathlon share the root, from Greek deka.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.hecto-: Hecto comes from Greek for hundred, and hectares and hectopascals, used in weather forecasts, are examples.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.kilo-: Kilo is from the Greek for thousand; the kilogram is the only SI base unit that has a prefix in its name.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.mega-: Mega means great in Greek, and a megabyte is a million bytes, and megapixels measure your phone's camera.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.giga-: Giga refers to giant in Greek, and gigabytes and gigahertz are everyday measures of storage and speed.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.tera-: Tera comes from the Greek for monster, and a terabyte of storage can hold hundreds of hours of video.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.peta-: Peta is a quadrillion, and the biggest data centers store petabytes, equal to millions of gigabytes.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.exa-: Exa is a quintillion, and a computer performing an exaflop does a billion billion calculations per second.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.zetta-: Zetta is a sextillion, and the world's total digital data is measured in zettabytes.
Big SI prefixes, by the size they mean.yotta-: Yotta is a septillion, and as the largest official prefix for decades, it was meant to be hard to reach, until 2022 when ronna and quetta were added.

The future year each sci-fi film is set.Escape from New York: Escape from New York is set in the then-future 1997, when Manhattan has become a maximum-security prison island.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.2001: A Space Odyssey: Kubrick's film has HAL 9000 and a mission to Jupiter, and it was set in a year that came and went long ago.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.Back to the Future Part II: The film predicted hoverboards, self-lacing shoes and flying cars, and Marty McFly arrives on October 21, 2015.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.Blade Runner (1982): This film's Los Angeles of 2019 has neon skies and flying cars, and it asks what separates humans from replicants.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.Children of Men: Alfonso Cuarón's film shows a world where no children have been born for 18 years, and is known for its extended one-shot scenes.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.Demolition Man: Sylvester Stallone plays a cop thawed from cryogenic prison in a peaceful 2032 San Angeles, and it popularized seashells for toilet use.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.Blade Runner 2049: The sequel takes place 30 years after the original, and features Ryan Gosling's blade runner K, and earned an Oscar for cinematography.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.Total Recall (1990): Arnold Schwarzenegger travels to Mars in a film based on a Philip K. Dick story, and its 2084 colony has a corrupt mining company.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.Idiocracy: Mike Judge's comedy imagines humans getting dumber over centuries, and a man wakes up in a world run by idiots.
The future year each sci-fi film is set.WALL-E: WALL-E is set in a future where humans have left Earth, and a lonely robot cleans up the garbage left behind.

Heights of London landmarks.Nelson's Column: The statue on top is Admiral Nelson at Trafalgar, and the four bronze lions at its base were added decades later, by Landseer.
Heights of London landmarks.Tower Bridge: It is often mistaken for London Bridge, which sits upstream and is a plain, unremarkable structure.
Heights of London landmarks.Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben): Big Ben is actually the great bell inside, not the tower itself; the tower was renamed for Queen Elizabeth II in 2012.
Heights of London landmarks.St. Paul's Cathedral: It was London's tallest building for over 250 years, until the early 1960s.
Heights of London landmarks.The Walkie-Talkie: Its concave glass once focused sunlight so intensely in 2013 that it melted parts of a parked car, earning the nickname Fryscraper.
Heights of London landmarks.The Gherkin: Officially 30 St Mary Axe, it was designed by Norman Foster and its curved profile helps ease the wind at street level.
Heights of London landmarks.The Leadenhall Building: Its sloping wedge shape, which earned it the name Cheesegrater, was designed to protect views of St Paul's Cathedral.
Heights of London landmarks.One Canada Square: For two decades this Canary Wharf tower, topped by a pyramid, was Britain's tallest building, until the Shard overtook it.
Heights of London landmarks.22 Bishopsgate: Completed in 2019, it is the tallest building in the City of London and has a rooftop viewing and public gardens planned inside.
Heights of London landmarks.The Shard: Renzo Piano's glass spire opened in 2012 and is the tallest building in the UK, shaped like a shard of glass.

When these fell.Tenochtitlan: The Aztec capital rose from an island in a lake and may have had 200,000 people. Cortés took it after a siege, and smallpox weakened its defenders.
When these fell.The Bastille: The fortress prison held only seven prisoners when stormed on 14 July 1789, but the day became France's national holiday.
When these fell.Holy Roman Empire: Voltaire had joked that it was neither holy, Roman, nor an empire; Napoleon pressured Francis II to dissolve it.
When these fell.Qing dynasty: The last emperor, Puyi, abdicated at the age of six, ending more than 2,000 years of imperial rule in China.
When these fell.Ottoman sultanate: Turkey's new assembly abolished the sultanate in 1922, and the caliphate followed in 1924.
When these fell.Saigon: The fall of the South Vietnamese capital on 30 April 1975 ended the war; the city was later renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
When these fell.The Shah of Iran: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi left Iran in January 1979, shortly before Ayatollah Khomeini returned in triumph.
When these fell.The Berlin Wall: A press-conference blunder by an East German official led crowds to rush the checkpoints on 9 November 1989.
When these fell.The Soviet Union: Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991, and the flag came down over the Kremlin, ending the superpower.
When these fell.Saddam Hussein's regime: The toppling of his statue in Baghdad's Firdos Square became the war's defining image, and he was captured that December.

Heading out from the Sun's core.Core: Fusion here turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second, at about 15 million degrees Celsius.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Radiative zone: Light takes up to hundreds of thousands of years to zigzag out through this dense layer.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Convection zone: Hot gas rises and cooler gas sinks like boiling water, making the grainy texture visible on the Sun's surface.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Photosphere: At about 5,500 degrees Celsius, this is where sunspots appear, cooler regions that look dark.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Chromosphere: Helium was first detected here in 1868, in sunlight during an eclipse, before being found on Earth.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Corona: It is hundreds of times hotter than the surface, a puzzle solar physicists still investigate; the Parker Solar Probe flew through it.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Kuiper Belt: It is home to Pluto and other icy bodies beyond Neptune.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Termination shock: Voyager 1 crossed it around 2004, where the solar wind abruptly slows.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Heliopause: Voyager 1 crossed it in 2012, becoming the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space.
Heading out from the Sun's core.Oort Cloud: It has never been directly observed, but is thought to be the source of long-period comets.

Total playing pieces in a standard set.Ludo: Ludo descends from India's Pachisi, and each of the four players races four tokens around the board.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Checkers: Called draughts in Britain; in 2007 the Chinook program proved that perfect play always ends in a draw.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Dominoes (double-six): A double-six set has 28 tiles; the game reached Europe in the 1700s, probably from China via Italy.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Backgammon: Its ancestors are about 5,000 years old, and the doubling cube was added by 1920s New York players.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Chess: There are more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe, an estimate called the Shannon number.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Connect Four: The 7-by-6 grid takes exactly 42 discs to fill, and the first player can always win with perfect play, as shown in 1988.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Jenga: Its name comes from the Swahili word for build, and the game was created by Leslie Scott, who grew up in Africa.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Stratego: Hidden ranks make it a game of bluff; it derives from an older French game called L'Attaque.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Scrabble (English): Alfred Butts designed it after counting letter frequencies on the front pages of The New York Times, which is why tiles differ in number.
Total playing pieces in a standard set.Go: The game is over 2,500 years old and AlphaGo's 2016 win over Lee Sedol stunned experts who thought computers were decades away.

Great droughts through history.Maya collapse droughts: Lake and cave sediment records suggest multi-year droughts coincided with the collapse of southern lowland Maya cities.
Great droughts through history.Great Famine drought (Asia): El Niño droughts hit India, China and Brazil, killing millions; British colonial policy worsened the toll in India.
Great droughts through history.Dust Bowl: Ploughing up prairie grass left soil to blow away. 'Black blizzards' carried dust as far as Washington, D.C.
Great droughts through history.Sahel drought: Rains failed across the semi-arid belt south of the Sahara, killing hundreds of thousands.
Great droughts through history.Ethiopian famine drought: Its famine inspired the Live Aid concerts of 1985.
Great droughts through history.Australia's Millennium Drought: Australia's longest dry spell ended with the 2010-11 floods and spurred desalination plants.
Great droughts through history.Horn of Africa drought: Famine was declared in parts of Somalia, with UN estimates of around a quarter of a million deaths.
Great droughts through history.California drought: The snowpack hit record lows, and the governor ordered mandatory water cuts in 2015.
Great droughts through history.Cape Town's Day Zero crisis: 'Day Zero', the day taps would be shut off, was avoided only by sharply cutting water use.
Great droughts through history.Panama Canal drought: Low water in Gatun Lake forced canal authorities to limit daily ship crossings.

Bollywood landmarks by release.Mother India: Mother India was the first Indian film nominated for the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film. It's a story of a poor villager mother.
Bollywood landmarks by release.Mughal-e-Azam: This epic took nearly 15 years to complete, and its grand palace set featured a hall of mirrors. It was rereleased in colour in 2004.
Bollywood landmarks by release.Sholay: The "curry western" ran in a Mumbai cinema for more than five years. Gabbar Singh remains Bollywood's most quoted villain.
Bollywood landmarks by release.Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge: Shah Rukh Khan and Kajol's romance ran in a Mumbai cinema for over 20 years, until the pandemic. It's among the longest theatrical runs ever.
Bollywood landmarks by release.Kuch Kuch Hota Hai: It was Karan Johar's first film as director. Its blend of friendship and romance shaped college-style fashion for years.
Bollywood landmarks by release.Lagaan: A village cricket match against British officers decides the fate of a tax. It received an Oscar nomination for Best Foreign Language Film.
Bollywood landmarks by release.Devdas (Shah Rukh Khan): Based on a 1917 Bengali novel, it was a lavish Sanjay Leela Bhansali take on a tale filmed many times. Its sets were extravagantly large.
Bollywood landmarks by release.3 Idiots: This comedy about engineering students was inspired in part by a Chetan Bhagat novel. A phrase from it, "All is well," became a catchphrase.
Bollywood landmarks by release.Dangal: Aamir Khan plays a former wrestler who trains his daughters, based on the real Phogat family. It was a huge hit in China.
Bollywood landmarks by release.RRR: This Telugu action epic by S. S. Rajamouli won an Oscar for Best Original Song for "Naatu Naatu." It's one of the highest-grossing Indian films.

How many are alive today?.Vaquita: The world's rarest marine mammal, a small porpoise found only in the northern Gulf of California. Fishing nets that entangle it have driven it close to extinction.
How many are alive today?.Amur leopard: Among the rarest big cats, it lives in the far east of Russia and nearby China. Its thick, pale coat helps it survive harsh winters.
How many are alive today?.Giant panda (wild): Pandas have a bamboo diet but retain a carnivore's gut. China's conservation work led to the species being downgraded from endangered to vulnerable in 2016.
How many are alive today?.Tiger (wild): A century ago there were perhaps 100,000 wild tigers, and today only a few thousand remain. Recent numbers have started to recover in places like India and Nepal.
How many are alive today?.Lion (wild): Lions have vanished from most of their historical range, and now live mainly in sub-Saharan Africa, with a small group in India's Gir Forest.
How many are alive today?.African elephant: Both the savanna and forest species are under threat from poaching and habitat loss. Their numbers have fallen by well over half in recent decades.
How many are alive today?.Sheep: There are more sheep than people in countries like New Zealand and Australia. They were among the first animals domesticated, roughly 10,000 years ago.
How many are alive today?.Humans: The population passed 8 billion in late 2022. It took until about 1804 to reach the first billion, and then only around 200 years to add the rest.
How many are alive today?.Chickens: The most numerous bird by far, outnumbering humans roughly three to one. They descend from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia.
How many are alive today?.Ants: Scientists estimate there are about 20 quadrillion ants, so their combined weight rivals that of all humans. They live on every continent except Antarctica.

How much water these use or hold.Cup of tea: Tea is the most widely drunk beverage after water. Tea bags were popularised in the early 1900s, reputedly by accident, when a New York merchant sent samples in silk bags.
How much water these use or hold.Full kettle: A kettle full of water takes a surprising amount of energy to boil, so boiling only what you need is a simple saving. Electric kettles became common in the 20th century.
How much water these use or hold.Toilet flush: Older toilets could use 13 litres a flush, and modern ones use around 6 or fewer. Flushing is typically one of the largest uses of water in a home.
How much water these use or hold.Dishwasher load: A modern dishwasher often uses less water than washing the same dishes by hand. The first practical machine was invented by Josephine Cochrane in the 1880s.
How much water these use or hold.Washing machine load: Efficient machines use far less water than older ones. The first electric washers appeared in the early 20th century and changed domestic life.
How much water these use or hold.Eight-minute shower: A short shower uses much less than a bath, though a power shower can use much more. The shower itself is ancient, as the Greeks built communal ones.
How much water these use or hold.Bath: Bathing was a social activity for the Romans, who built grand public baths with heated pools. Today, a full bath often uses more water than a quick shower.
How much water these use or hold.Garden hose for an hour: Leaving a hose on can use as much water as a household needs in several days. This is why many places restrict hosepipe use in summer droughts.
How much water these use or hold.Hot tub: Hot tubs began as wooden barrels of heated water in California in the 1960s. They need chemicals to stay clean, since warm water encourages bacteria.
How much water these use or hold.Olympic pool: An Olympic pool is 50 metres long and at least two metres deep, and holds about 2.5 million litres. It takes a long time to fill.

A Christmas Carol, in story order.Scrooge snubs the charity men: Dickens published A Christmas Carol in December 1843, and the first printing sold out within days.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Marley's ghost appears: Marley's chains are forged from cash boxes, keys and ledgers, the things he lived for.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Ghost of Christmas Past: The Ghost of Christmas Past is often shown with a bright flame on its head, and a cap that can snuff it out.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Young Scrooge at Fezziwig's: Fezziwig shows a boss who spent little to give his workers a joyful evening, in contrast to Scrooge.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Ghost of Christmas Present: The Ghost of Christmas Present wears a green robe trimmed with fur and sits among piles of food, symbols of abundance.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Christmas with the Cratchits: The Cratchits eat a modest Christmas meal, with Tiny Tim's God bless us, every one! as the story's best-known line.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come: The final spirit never speaks and is shown as a hooded phantom, making it more frightening than the rest.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Scrooge sees his own grave: Dickens wrote the story partly as a protest against how London treated the poor, especially children.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Waking on Christmas morning: Humbug means a hoax or sham, and it is Scrooge's catchphrase for the whole holiday.
A Christmas Carol, in story order.Buying the prize turkey: The prize turkey is so big that Scrooge pays a boy to carry it, and it is the first spontaneous kindness he shows.

Boats and ships through history.Dugout canoe: The Pesse canoe, found in the Netherlands, is a hollowed-out pine log about 10,000 years old, among the oldest boats known.
Boats and ships through history.Sailboat: Egyptians drew sails on pottery around 3500 BC, and the Nile's current flowing north with winds blowing south made sailing easy.
Boats and ships through history.Greek trireme: Triremes had three banks of oars and around 170 rowers, and they fought famously at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC.
Boats and ships through history.Viking longship: Vikings sailed shallow longships that could cross the Atlantic and also be hauled up rivers, reaching North America around 1000.
Boats and ships through history.Spanish galleon: Spanish galleons carried silver from the Americas back to Spain, making them tempting targets for English and Dutch privateers.
Boats and ships through history.Fulton's steamboat: Robert Fulton's Clermont steamed up the Hudson from New York to Albany in 1807, making steam travel commercially practical.
Boats and ships through history.Clipper ship: The Cutty Sark, built in 1869, is the most famous clipper; clippers raced home with tea and wool using huge sail areas.
Boats and ships through history.Titanic: Titanic carried only 20 lifeboats, which had room for about half of those aboard, despite meeting the regulations of the time.
Boats and ships through history.Nuclear submarine: USS Nautilus in 1954 was the first nuclear-powered submarine, and could stay submerged for months instead of hours.
Boats and ships through history.Hovercraft: The SR.N1 hovercraft crossed the English Channel in 1959, riding a cushion of air that made it work over land and water.

Irish writers, by birth year.Jonathan Swift: The Dublin-born satirist wrote Gulliver's Travels and once proposed, as dark irony, that the poor sell their children as food.
Irish writers, by birth year.Laurence Sterne: Born in Clonmel, he wrote the madcap novel Tristram Shandy, which plays with the form so boldly it feels strangely modern.
Irish writers, by birth year.Bram Stoker: Before Dracula, he worked as the business manager of London's Lyceum Theatre, serving the famous actor Henry Irving.
Irish writers, by birth year.Oscar Wilde: The wit behind The Importance of Being Earnest wrote only one novel, The Picture of Dorian Gray, and spent time in Reading Gaol.
Irish writers, by birth year.George Bernard Shaw: He won the Nobel Prize in Literature and an Oscar for Pygmalion's screenplay, the only person to win both.
Irish writers, by birth year.W. B. Yeats: The poet won the Nobel Prize in 1923 and served as a senator in the new Irish Free State.
Irish writers, by birth year.James Joyce: His novel Ulysses follows a single day in Dublin, June 16, 1904, now celebrated every year as Bloomsday.
Irish writers, by birth year.Samuel Beckett: Best known for Waiting for Godot, he wrote in both French and English and won the Nobel Prize in 1969.
Irish writers, by birth year.Seamus Heaney: The Nobel-winning poet often wrote about the Irish countryside, digging into peat bogs, farm life and memory.
Irish writers, by birth year.Sally Rooney: Her novels Normal People and Conversations with Friends made her a leading voice of millennial fiction, and the former was adapted for TV.
